The nestling period is remarkably brief, with the age at birth recorded at 13 days [ab = 13 days] when eggs are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], though some sources extend this to 14-15 days under variable thermal regimes. During the first few days post-hatching, the newly emerged chick is entirely dependent on its parents for brooding and provisioning, with the initial wet weight of the newly laid egg recorded at 1.86 grams [Ww0 = 1.86 grams], indicating a relatively large egg for the bird's body size. This yolk-dependent embryo absorbs the albumen-buffered nutrients to fuel the rapid organogenesis that characterizes this species' early life history.

As the nestling chick develops, it undergoes an extraordinary phase of mass gain, building toward an ultimate wet weight of 12.6 grams [Wwi = 12.6 grams] by the time it achieves adult body mass. This relatively delayed onset of gonadal maturation allows the juvenile bird to complete its post-fledging dispersal and establish familiarity with its natal territory before investing in reproduction. The typical juvenile bird spends several weeks as a growing immature individual, refining its foraging skills on aerial insects, before the gonad maturation process begins in earnest, triggered by photoperiodic cues and prey availability.
